lec05kp07-u01-p1-title.name: u01-p1-title
lec05kp07-u01-p1-title.text: Training repeats four steps: start values once, then forward, backward and update each epoch

lec05kp07-u01-p1-bridge.name: u01-p1-bridge
lec05kp07-u01-p1-bridge.text: KP06 took one step with a single sample. Real training has many samples, for example the four XOR points: when are the weights updated, and how does the whole procedure fit together?

lec05kp07-u01-p1-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp07-loop
lec05kp07-u01-p1-fig1.text: The training loop: forward pass, compute error, backpropagate, update weights, repeated until the stop rule; one pass over the N=4 samples is one epoch.

image.alt: The training loop: forward pass, compute error, backpropagate, update weights, repeated until the stop rule; one pass over the N=4 samples is one epoch.

lec05kp07-u01-p1-term:epoch.name: term:Epoch
lec05kp07-u01-p1-term:epoch.text: **Epoch**: presenting all $N$ training samples once. Here $N=4$ (the four XOR points).

lec05kp07-u01-p1-term:批次訓練.name: term:Batch training
lec05kp07-u01-p1-term:批次訓練.text: **Batch training**: in one epoch every sample first gets its $\delta$ and the sum updates the weights once: $\Delta w=\eta\sum_i\delta(i)\,y^{r-1}(i)\,/N$. Dividing by $N$ only rescales $\eta$.

lec05kp07-u01-p1-c.name: u01-p1-c
lec05kp07-u01-p1-c.text: **Four steps**: 1 initialize (small random values, once); 2 forward and store values; 3 backward for the $\delta$ of every sample; 4 update. Repeat 2 to 4 until stopping.

lec05kp07-u01-p2-title.name: u01-p2-title
lec05kp07-u01-p2-title.text: Epoch 1: the four points go forward first, J = 0.0084

lec05kp07-u01-p2-bridge.name: u01-p2-bridge
lec05kp07-u01-p2-bridge.text: The four steps start every epoch with the forward pass. With the source's 2-2-1 network and initial weights, what output does each XOR point get?

lec05kp07-u01-p2-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp07-epoch1-forward
lec05kp07-u01-p2-fig1.text: Forward pass of the first epoch: the four XOR outputs are 0.2578, 0.9851, 0.9851 and 0.0043, cost J=0.0084, all on the correct side of 0.5.

image.alt: Forward pass of the first epoch: the four XOR outputs are 0.2578, 0.9851, 0.9851 and 0.0043, cost J=0.0084, all on the correct side of 0.5.

lec05kp07-u01-p2-c1.name: u01-p2-c1
lec05kp07-u01-p2-c1.text: **Weights** (bias, $x_1$, $x_2$): hidden unit 1 $(-2,5,5)$, unit 2 $(-7,5,5)$, output $(-2,8,-12)$, the initial setting of the source's interactive example.

lec05kp07-u01-p2-c2.name: u01-p2-c2
lec05kp07-u01-p2-c2.text: **Result**: $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$ give $0.2578$ and $0.0043$ (target 0); $(0,1)$ and $(1,0)$ give $0.9851$ (target 1). All four are on the right side.

lec05kp07-u01-p2-c3.name: u01-p2-c3
lec05kp07-u01-p2-c3.text: **Cost** $J$ is the mean of $\tfrac12(\text{target}-o)^2$ over the four samples: $J=0.0084$.

lec05kp07-u01-p3-title.name: u01-p3-title
lec05kp07-u01-p3-title.text: Each sample gets its δ, the sum is averaged and times η updates once: all nine weights move a little

lec05kp07-u01-p3-bridge.name: u01-p3-bridge
lec05kp07-u01-p3-bridge.text: The outputs of the four points are known and J is 0.0084. After this update, how do the $\delta$ of the four samples combine into one update?

lec05kp07-u01-p3-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp07-epoch1-update
lec05kp07-u01-p3-fig1.text: The nine weight updates of the first epoch (η=1.5, averaged over four samples); J goes from 0.00837 to 0.00799.

image.alt: The nine weight updates of the first epoch (η=1.5, averaged over four samples); J goes from 0.00837 to 0.00799.

lec05kp07-u01-p3-c2.name: u01-p3-c2
lec05kp07-u01-p3-c2.text: **Sum, then average**: $\Delta w=\eta\cdot(\text{sum over the four samples of }\delta\times\text{input})/4$ with $\eta=1.5$. For example the output bias moves $-0.0183$ and hidden unit 1's bias $-0.0155$.

lec05kp07-u01-p3-c3.name: u01-p3-c3
lec05kp07-u01-p3-c3.text: **After the update**: $J$ goes from $0.00837$ to $0.00799$; one epoch is a small step.

lec05kp07-u01-p4-title.name: u01-p4-title
lec05kp07-u01-p4-title.text: Repeating epoch after epoch: J needs 3707 epochs to fall below 0.0002

lec05kp07-u01-p4-bridge.name: u01-p4-bridge
lec05kp07-u01-p4-bridge.text: One epoch moves all nine weights a little. If we keep repeating epoch after epoch, how does J move and when should we stop?

lec05kp07-u01-p4-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp07-curve
lec05kp07-u01-p4-fig1.text: Log curve of the cost J against epochs: 0.00799, 0.00567, 0.00175 and 0.00046 at epochs 1, 10, 100, 1000, crossing the 0.0002 threshold at epoch 3707.

image.alt: Log curve of the cost J against epochs: 0.00799, 0.00567, 0.00175 and 0.00046 at epochs 1, 10, 100, 1000, crossing the 0.0002 threshold at epoch 3707.

lec05kp07-u01-p4-term:停止條件.name: term:Stop rule
lec05kp07-u01-p4-term:停止條件.text: **Stop rule**: the cost $J$ falls below a threshold, or the gradient becomes almost zero. Here $J<0.0002$ and all four points correct.

lec05kp07-u01-p4-c1.name: u01-p4-c1
lec05kp07-u01-p4-c1.text: **The course**: $J$ at epochs 1, 10, 100 and 1000 is $0.00799$, $0.00567$, $0.00175$ and $0.00046$, and it falls below $0.0002$ only at epoch 3707.

lec05kp07-u01-p5-title.name: u01-p5-title
lec05kp07-u01-p5-title.text: A small learning rate needs tens of thousands of epochs and a huge one overshoots at once

lec05kp07-u01-p5-bridge.name: u01-p5-bridge
lec05kp07-u01-p5-bridge.text: Epoch after epoch, J needs 3707 epochs to fall below 0.0002. Can we make the learning rate larger?

lec05kp07-u01-p5-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp07-eta-bars
lec05kp07-u01-p5-fig1.text: Learning rate against epochs needed: 55607 for η=0.1, 11121 for 0.5, 3707 for 1.5, 1853 for 3, 926 for 6, 185 for 30, 53 for 100, and η=200 fails.

image.alt: Learning rate against epochs needed: 55607 for η=0.1, 11121 for 0.5, 3707 for 1.5, 1853 for 3, 926 for 6, 185 for 30, 53 for 100, and η=200 fails.

lec05kp07-u01-p5-c1.name: u01-p5-c1
lec05kp07-u01-p5-c1.text: **Example**: $\eta=0.1$ needs 55607 epochs, $1.5$ needs 3707, $6$ needs 926 and $100$ needs 53.

lec05kp07-u01-p5-c2.name: u01-p5-c2
lec05kp07-u01-p5-c2.text: **Too large**: with $\eta=200$ $J$ rises in the first two steps and ends with all four outputs $1.00$, $J=0.25$ and only 2 points correct (program).

lec05kp07-u01-p5-c3.name: u01-p5-c3
lec05kp07-u01-p5-c3.text: **Why**: the best $\eta$ depends on the shape of the cost in weight space: wide flat minima allow big steps, steep narrow ones need small steps (source).

lec05kp07-u01-p6-title.name: u01-p6-title
lec05kp07-u01-p6-title.text: The start cannot be all zeros: every gradient is exactly 0 and J stays at 0.125

lec05kp07-u01-p6-bridge.name: u01-p6-bridge
lec05kp07-u01-p6-bridge.text: A learning rate that is too small or too large fails, and a good one makes training move. But where does training start? What if all weights start at 0?

lec05kp07-u01-p6-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp07-zero-init
lec05kp07-u01-p6-fig1.text: With all weights 0 the cost stays at J=0.125 forever, compared with the falling curve from ordinary initial values.

image.alt: With all weights 0 the cost stays at J=0.125 forever, compared with the falling curve from ordinary initial values.

lec05kp07-u01-p6-term:初始化.name: term:Initialization
lec05kp07-u01-p6-term:初始化.text: **Initialization**: before training every weight gets a starting value, usually small random values (from a pseudo-random generator).

lec05kp07-u01-p6-c1.name: u01-p6-c1
lec05kp07-u01-p6-c1.text: **What all zeros does**: every output is $0.5$; the output-layer $\delta$ of the four samples cancel and the hidden $\delta$ is multiplied by the output weights (0), so every gradient is exactly 0, so $J=0.125$ never moves (program).

lec05kp07-u01-p6-c2.name: u01-p6-c2
lec05kp07-u01-p6-c2.text: **Small random values**: 20 random starts in $\pm0.5$ with $\eta=1.5$ all reached $J<0.0002$, taking 10890 to 23926 epochs.

lec05kp07-u01-p7-title.name: u01-p7-title
lec05kp07-u01-p7-title.text: Another start can get stuck at J=0.0626 with almost zero gradient, and waiting does not help

lec05kp07-u01-p7-bridge.name: u01-p7-bridge
lec05kp07-u01-p7-bridge.text: Small random values mostly reach the end. If the random values are larger, can some starts fail to arrive?

lec05kp07-u01-p7-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp07-stuck
lec05kp07-u01-p7-fig1.text: Cost curves of two starts: start A stalls at J=0.0626 (outputs 0.01, 0.99, 0.5, 0.5) and start B converges in 8204 epochs.

image.alt: Cost curves of two starts: start A stalls at J=0.0626 (outputs 0.01, 0.99, 0.5, 0.5) and start B converges in 8204 epochs.

lec05kp07-u01-p7-term:區域極小值.name: term:Local minimum
lec05kp07-u01-p7-term:區域極小值.text: **Local minimum**: lowest nearby but not lowest overall, with zero gradient, so gradient descent cannot leave it. Backpropagation can get trapped.

lec05kp07-u01-p7-c1.name: u01-p7-c1
lec05kp07-u01-p7-c1.text: **Example**: 300 random starts with weights in $\pm3$, $\eta=3$, at most 20000 epochs: 176 reached the goal and 124 did not.

lec05kp07-u01-p7-c2.name: u01-p7-c2
lec05kp07-u01-p7-c2.text: **What stuck looks like**: start A sits at $J=0.0626$ with outputs $0.01,\ 0.99,\ 0.5,\ 0.5$ and a gradient of length only $3\times10^{-5}$; 60000 more epochs did not leave.

lec05kp07-u01-p8-title.name: u01-p8-title
lec05kp07-u01-p8-title.text: Updating after every sample cuts the epochs, but a stuck start stays stuck

lec05kp07-u01-p8-bridge.name: u01-p8-bridge
lec05kp07-u01-p8-bridge.text: Another start can get stuck at $J=0.0626$ with almost zero gradient, and waiting does not help. Must we change the start? Another method updates after every sample, so can it jump out?

lec05kp07-u01-p8-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp07-batch-pattern
lec05kp07-u01-p8-fig1.text: Epochs of three setups: batch η=1.5 needs 3707, pattern η=1.5 needs 924, batch η=6 needs 926; from the stuck start all three remain at J≈0.0626 after 20000 epochs.

image.alt: Epochs of three setups: batch η=1.5 needs 3707, pattern η=1.5 needs 924, batch η=6 needs 926; from the stuck start all three remain at J≈0.0626 after 20000 epochs.

lec05kp07-u01-p8-term:逐筆訓練.name: term:Pattern training
lec05kp07-u01-p8-term:逐筆訓練.text: **Pattern (online) training**: after every sample update with that sample's $\delta$: $w\leftarrow w+\eta\,\delta\,y^{r-1}$. It is noisier and the source says it may jump out of a local minimum.

lec05kp07-u01-p8-c1.name: u01-p8-c1
lec05kp07-u01-p8-c1.text: **Example** (source weights): pattern $\eta=1.5$ needs 924 epochs, batch $\eta=1.5$ needs 3707, batch $\eta=6$ (same total step) needs 926.

lec05kp07-u01-p8-c2.name: u01-p8-c2
lec05kp07-u01-p8-c2.text: **Stuck start A**: pattern mode (fixed or shuffled) is still at $J\approx0.063$ after 20000 epochs; it did not escape. 'May' is no guarantee.

lec05kp07-u01-p9-title.name: u01-p9-title
lec05kp07-u01-p9-title.text: Extension: after training the weights are frozen and classifying needs only multiply-adds and a sigmoid

lec05kp07-u01-p9-bridge.name: u01-p9-bridge
lec05kp07-u01-p9-bridge.text: Updating after every sample cuts the epochs, but training still takes many epochs to converge. Once it has converged the weights stop changing, so how much work does classifying cost?

lec05kp07-u01-p9-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp07-frozen
lec05kp07-u01-p9-fig1.text: The nine frozen weights after training and the outputs 0.029, 0.982, 0.982 and 0.010 for the four inputs.

image.alt: The nine frozen weights after training and the outputs 0.029, 0.982, 0.982 and 0.010 for the four inputs.

lec05kp07-u01-p9-term:凍結權重.name: term:Frozen weights
lec05kp07-u01-p9-term:凍結權重.text: **Frozen weights**: after training the weights are no longer updated and classifying only needs multiply-adds and the sigmoid.

lec05kp07-u01-p9-c1.name: u01-p9-c1
lec05kp07-u01-p9-c1.text: **Here**: 9 weights, 6 multiplications and 3 sigmoids per input, with outputs $0.0292,\ 0.9821,\ 0.9821,\ 0.0103$.

lec05kp07-u01-p9-c2.name: u01-p9-c2
lec05kp07-u01-p9-c2.text: **Parallelism**: units in one layer are independent, hence optical, VLSI and dedicated neural-computer implementations (source).

lec05kp07-u01-p10-title.name: u01-p10-title
lec05kp07-u01-p10-title.text: Extension: practice, one pattern-mode step on the sample (0,0)

lec05kp07-u01-p10-bridge.name: u01-p10-bridge
lec05kp07-u01-p10-bridge.text: Before the weights are frozen every step updates them. Pattern mode updates after one sample: with only $(0,0)$, what are the output-layer $\delta_o$ and the three weight updates?

lec05kp07-u01-p10-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp07-practice-forward
lec05kp07-u01-p10-fig1.text: Practice figure: forward pass of sample (0,0), hidden outputs 0.1192 and 0.0009, output 0.2578, target 0.

image.alt: Practice figure: forward pass of sample (0,0), hidden outputs 0.1192 and 0.0009, output 0.2578, target 0.

lec05kp07-u01-p10-q1.name: u01-p10-q1
lec05kp07-u01-p10-q1.text: **Question 1**: with only $(0,0)$ (target 0), what is the output-layer $\delta_o$?

lec05kp07-u01-p10-h1.name: u01-p10-h1
lec05kp07-u01-p10-h1.text: **Hint**: $\delta_o=(\text{target}-o)\,f'(v_o)$ and $f'(v_o)=o(1-o)$; the forward numbers are in the figure.

lec05kp07-u01-p10-q2.name: u01-p10-q2
lec05kp07-u01-p10-q2.text: **Question 2**: what are the updates of the three output-layer weights ($\eta=1.5$)?

lec05kp07-u01-p11-title.name: u01-p11-title
lec05kp07-u01-p11-title.text: Extension: worked solution of questions 1 and 2

lec05kp07-u01-p11-bridge.name: u01-p11-bridge
lec05kp07-u01-p11-bridge.text: The practice asked for $\delta_o$ and the three updates from the sample $(0,0)$. Worked out in full, what are the answers?

lec05kp07-u01-p11-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp07-practice-sol
lec05kp07-u01-p11-fig1.text: Output-layer updates for sample (0,0): bias −0.0740, from hidden 1 −0.0088, from hidden 2 −0.0001.

image.alt: Output-layer updates for sample (0,0): bias −0.0740, from hidden 1 −0.0088, from hidden 2 −0.0001.

lec05kp07-u01-p11-a3.name: u01-p11-a3
lec05kp07-u01-p11-a3.text: **Check**: the target is 0 and the output 0.2578 is too high, so the output weights go down; hidden unit 1 has $\delta=-0.0414$ and its bias moves $-0.0622$.

steps.label: Backprop algorithm
steps.speakerNotes: Level: undergraduate (year 3). Main line 8 pages plus 3 extension pages (not timed). Self-study deck, English version. Made under CLARITY.md C12 to C18. It uses real numbers of the source's interactive example (XOR, a fixed 2-2-1 network and its initial weights); all epoch counts and outputs were recomputed by a program, and the stuck and all-zero starts are this lecture's own program experiments (added). These notes are public with the file and contain no student IDs, grades or exam questions.

steps.label: The four steps
steps.speakerNotes: KP06 took one step with a single sample. This page asks when the weights are updated when there are many training samples. Two words first: an epoch is presenting all N training samples once, here N is 4, the four XOR points; batch training means that in one epoch every sample first gets its delta and the sum updates the weights once, where dividing by N only rescales the learning rate. The procedure has four steps: initialize with small random values once, then in every epoch go forward and store the values, go backward for the delta of every sample, and update once, repeating until the stop rule holds. The arrow on the left of the figure is this loop. The next page takes the source's 2-2-1 network and initial weights and walks through the first epoch.

steps.label: Epoch 1: forward
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said every epoch starts with the forward pass. This page uses the source's 2-2-1 network and initial weights: hidden unit 1 is (-2, 5, 5), unit 2 is (-7, 5, 5) and the output is (-2, 8, -12). Each of the four points goes forward: (0,0) gives 0.2578 and (1,1) gives 0.0043 with target 0; (0,1) and (1,0) give 0.9851 with target 1. All four are on the right side of 0.5, and the cost J, the mean of one half of the squared target minus output over the four samples, is 0.0084. The figure lists the hidden outputs and the final output of every point. The next page shows how the four samples combine into one update.

steps.label: Epoch 1: backward, update
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page finished the forward pass of the four points. This page does the backward pass and the update. Each of the four samples computes its output-layer delta: minus 0.0493 for (0,0), 0.0002 each for (0,1) and (1,0), and about minus 0.00002 for (1,1). The hidden-layer deltas are computed backward as in KP06. Then the delta times input of the four samples is summed, divided by 4 and multiplied by the learning rate 1.5, and one epoch updates only once: the output bias moves minus 0.0183, hidden unit 1's bias moves minus 0.0155 and the rest are smaller, with the shading showing the size. After the update J goes from 0.00837 to 0.00799, one epoch being a small step. The next page asks how J behaves when we repeat.

steps.label: J falls to the bar
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page lowered J only a little per epoch. This page asks how J moves and when to stop. The figure plots J against epoch with both axes logarithmic: J at epochs 1, 10, 100 and 1000 is 0.00799, 0.00567, 0.00175 and 0.00046, and it falls below 0.0002 only at epoch 3707. Two stop rules are common: the cost falls below a threshold, or the gradient becomes almost zero; here J below 0.0002 and all four points correct. The outputs after training are 0.029, 0.982, 0.982 and 0.010 with targets 0, 1, 1, 0. These epoch counts were recomputed by a program. The next page asks whether a larger learning rate can shorten the 3707 epochs.

steps.label: The learning-rate dilemma
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page needed 3707 epochs to converge. This page asks whether the learning rate can be larger. The figure shows the number of epochs for different learning rates: 0.1 needs 55607, 1.5 needs 3707, 6 needs 926 and 100 needs only 53, so a larger rate is indeed faster. But too large fails: with a learning rate of 200 J rises in the first two steps and ends with all four outputs equal to 1, J equal to 0.25 and only two points correct. Why this dilemma? The source says the best learning rate depends on the shape of the cost in weight space: wide flat minima allow big steps and steep narrow ones need small steps, otherwise we overshoot. These epoch counts were recomputed by a program. The next page asks where training starts from.

steps.label: Not all zeros
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said training moves only with a good learning rate. This page asks where training starts. Initialization gives every weight a starting value before training, usually small random values. If all are set to 0 every output is 0.5, the deltas of the four samples cancel, every gradient is exactly 0 and J stays at 0.125, the flat red line in the figure; the blue line is the source's initial weights for contrast. We also tried 20 small random starts in plus or minus 0.5 with learning rate 1.5, and all reached J below 0.0002, taking 10890 to 23926 epochs. These are program experiments, not the source's experiments. The next page asks whether larger random values can fail to arrive.

steps.label: Local minimum
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed small random starts all arrive. This page asks whether larger random values can fail to arrive. The source says local minima are the norm and that backpropagation can get trapped. We drew 300 random starts with weights in plus or minus 3, learning rate 3 and at most 20000 epochs: 176 reached the goal and 124 did not. In the figure the red line is one start A stuck at J equal to 0.0626 with outputs 0.01, 0.99, 0.5 and 0.5 and a gradient of length only 3 times 10 to the minus 5, which did not leave even after 60000 more epochs; the green line is another start B that arrives in 8204 epochs. Note that a point with almost zero gradient can be a local minimum or a plateau, and here we can only say that it does not move. The remedy is to rerun with another initial set. The next page asks whether per-sample updating can escape.

steps.label: Per-sample updates
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page left start A stuck at J equal to 0.0626. This page asks whether we must change the start. Another method, pattern or online training, updates after every sample with that sample's delta; it is noisier and the source says it may jump out of a local minimum. First speed: with the source's weights, pattern learning rate 1.5 needs 924 epochs and batch learning rate 1.5 needs 3707; but the batch averages, and batch learning rate 6 has the same total step as pattern 1.5 and needs 926 epochs, almost the same, so pattern mode is faster mainly because of the step size, not magic. Now the stuck start A: whether the order is fixed or shuffled every epoch, J is still about 0.063 after 20000 epochs, so here it did not escape. The source says may, not guaranteed; batch or pattern depends on the problem. The main line ends here and the extension follows.

steps.label: Extension: freezing
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said that pattern and batch both take many epochs to converge. This page asks how much work classifying costs once it has converged. The answer is that after training the weights are frozen and classifying only needs multiply-adds and a sigmoid, far cheaper than training. This example has 9 weights, 6 multiplications and 3 sigmoids per input, with outputs 0.0292, 0.9821, 0.9821 and 0.0103. Neural networks are naturally parallel, units in one layer are independent, hence optical, VLSI and dedicated neural-computer implementations, as the source says. This page is an extension and is not timed. The next page is a practice.

steps.label: Extension: practice
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said that once the weights are frozen only classification remains. This page returns to training and asks the students for one pattern-mode step: use only the sample (0,0) with target 0. The left figure gives the forward numbers, hidden outputs 0.1192 and 0.0009 and output 0.2578. Question 1: what is the output-layer delta; question 2: what are the updates of the three output-layer weights with learning rate 1.5. The hint is that delta is target minus output times the slope of the output. The next page gives the complete solution.

steps.label: Extension: solution
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page posed questions 1 and 2 and this page is the complete solution. Question 1: delta is target minus output times the slope, 0 minus 0.2578 times 0.2578 times 1 minus 0.2578, which is minus 0.0493. Question 2: each update is 1.5 times delta times the input, and the inputs are 1, 0.1192 and 0.0009: the bias moves minus 0.0740, the weight from hidden unit 1 minus 0.0088 and from unit 2 minus 0.0001. Check: the target is 0 and the output 0.2578 is too high, so the output weights go down; hidden unit 1 has delta minus 0.0414 and its bias moves minus 0.0622. KP07 ends here and the next KP covers the accelerated variants of backpropagation.

metadata.title: Pattern Recognition, Chapter 4, KP07: the backpropagation algorithm and practical points (undergraduate, self-study)
